rv.q: Battye rips away the padding that makes relationship stories boring, pinpointing the most painful bits with one biting word or look or phrase.
Lucy Morrison, the director, gives this strange and stealthy love story a sensationally good production.
What could descend into militant, wokey gobbledegook is served by Battye with a scathingly funny light touch.

As Tosh, Tanya Reynolds conveys how her own brain can sometimes bewilder or delight her; Rebekah Murrell is magnetic as the more confident Lou, and as Sally Rooney fan Fran, Letty Thomas brings pathos to a part that could have been a caricature.
Battye has questions about the patterns young women are expected to follow, and her writing is a triple-word-score delight.

But the play never fully coalesces. The winding of the first two-thirds is undercut by a final third that whips back and forth in a series of rapid plot developments that aren't given sufficient room to breathe.
Though messy and, at times, uncertain, Scenes With Girls is a reminder that friendships deserve as much effort as romantic relationships.
Like that play, this feels like a breath of bracing air, a real insight into the lives of the girls it depicts.
It is also as likely that other viewers will struggle to empathise with or find much enlightenment in the activities of a couple of ultimately selfish women, whose life interests are so narrow.
Scenes with Girls is like an exciting blast of fresh air blowing through the often stale world of contemporary new writing.
It's a wonderful tribute to the Royal Court Writers' group that it is able to take the germ of an idea, work with a talented writer and magical team, and create such a fine piece of work.
